text:
Chapter Twelve


Maggie had never wished more for an off switch for her brain. Her thoughts were always a jumbled mess of to-do lists, bits of poetry translation, and ideas for exam questions that she’d inevitably forget to write down. But now? She couldn’t get Arthur Taliesin out of her head, or the anxiety-inducing catalog of every single text message she had sent him over the weekend.


She wasn’t sure, exactly, how they’d fallen into this rhythm. When she left him on Friday afternoon, wholly unsure whether he’d make it back to Atlantia without wrecking that rusty old truck, any shred of confidence and certainty she had about their agreement vanished. As she’d walked back to her apartment, she’d repeated a steady litany of worries: I made a deal with Arthur Taliesin. No, I forced him to agree to it. Arthur Taliesin! Is this technically blackmail? I need to look up the definition of blackmail.


Then, when she didn’t hear from him for over an hour, she panicked and sent him that first text. She imagined having to drive along the winding highway to Atlantia, searching for the burning wreckage of his truck in swampy ditches. And because she’d never been able to keep quiet when she was nervous, she just kept texting him until he finally responded with that picture of his hand.


And, gods below, what had possessed him to do that? Maggie had a sudden understanding of what men were trying to achieve with pictures of other parts of their anatomy. Clearly, they should have been sending pictures of their hands all along. She had stared at the photo of his long, tapered fingers, his wide palm, the glimpse of his corded forearm beyond his wrist with her mouth agape. It was a work of art. It made her think inappropriate thoughts about what that hand could do, the places those fingers could go. It was absolutely ridiculous.


At least she could blame her frazzled brain for the text she sent him later in the evening when he asked her what she would be doing on Thursday night. Ideally, I’ll be horizontal…The moment she hit send, she yelped as she realized what she wrote and felt an overwhelming urge to dive into her phone to retrieve it before he read it. Unfortunately, it was marked read instantly, like he’d been staring at the screen waiting for her to message him. She swore, biting her lip as she waited for his response. Even though he took a very long time to type out an answer, he had ignored any accidental double entendre, to Maggie’s relief.


The rest of their conversation managed to be relatively normal, and she had finally sent a good-night text, vowing to not send him any more messages all weekend. But then, at an absurdly early hour on Saturday morning, he sent her an inexplicable picture of a little boy with a surprisingly large fish.


Maggie didn’t see the photo until she woke up, hours after he sent it. She didn’t know what to say back. It couldn’t have been meant for her. Could it? And if it wasn’t meant for her, shouldn’t she make him aware of the fact that he sent her a picture of a kid with a fish? She thought she recognized him as the same boy in the photo on Taliesin’s desk, the one who had Taliesin’s smile. Was this his way of revealing he had a son? Could Arthur Taliesin have a son she was unaware of?


Finally, as she deliberated what to say, an explanation arrived.




A. Taliesin: Sorry. Accidentally sent that to you.






Maggie: I see you’re getting this kid started young with the time-honored tradition of Men Posing with Fish.






A. Taliesin: I take my job as uncle very seriously.




Uncle. The other man in the framed photo on his desk must be his brother, then. She felt strangely relieved by the response, a feeling she didn’t want to explore. She was curious, too. What was Arthur Taliesin like as an uncle?


That thought had occupied most of her weekend, especially since no additional text messages came in from Taliesin, accidental or intentional. It was for the best, of course, but she still found herself checking her phone more than once to see if she missed anything.


Now, sitting at her desk on Monday morning, Maggie dreaded Taliesin walking through the door of their office. At least before she had known how to act around him. She had known what to expect. But, suddenly, the ground had shifted. Between their agreement, the texts, that photo of his hand…Maggie took a giant sip of coffee to calm her nerves just as Taliesin walked in, and promptly choked on it.


And then his hands were on her back, his palm hitting between her shoulder blades as she coughed. “All right?” he asked as she regained control. He had stopped patting her back, but he hadn’t removed his hand from between her shoulders.


“I’m fine,” she managed to croak as she glanced up at him. She gently shimmied her shoulders and sat up straight until he removed his hand. His lips quirked in a slight grin before he went to his desk and then seemed to immediately get lost in his own work.


She was relieved she didn’t have time to dwell on the way he’d touched her. Like they were comfortable with each other. And they definitely were not. But, soon, there was a steady stream of students, both hers and Taliesin’s, in and out of the office, turning in last-minute assignments and asking for help with exam prep. Maggie had made a sign-up sheet for fifteen-minute increments so there was little overlap, but if two students did show up at the same time, Maggie and Taliesin took turns holding meetings in the hallway. It was all very orderly. If anything had really changed between them, it was this effortless way they shared their space without any of the push and pull that had plagued Maggie since he moved in.


Taliesin’s students made themselves feel at home in Maggie’s office. She heard more than one compliment the warm lighting, and they all sank into her couch, snuggling with the handmade granny-square blanket she had draped across the back. She bit her tongue against gloating to Taliesin about how much his students seemed to love the fainting couch, and she was exceedingly proud of herself for her restraint.


His students also found the cart of goodies that she kept stocked with extra treats around exam time to help ease nerves. Taliesin first tried to keep them from taking anything, but the allure of Mothman-shaped stress balls and candies that burst through with lavender jelly was impossible to deny, and Maggie told Taliesin to go ahead and let them.


After one of his students left, Taliesin held up the remaining stress ball. “Where does one purchase bug man stress balls? I need to refill your cart.”


Maggie’s first, annoying instinct was to tell him not to worry about it, but she squashed it. “I found them at Glinda’s,” Maggie explained, naming the tchotchke shop downtown that always had a delightful and strange assortment of treasures.


“Huh,” Taliesin said, turning a Mothman in his hand and squeezing it until its eyes bugged out. “I’ve never been there.”


Maggie thought about being mean to him. She really did. Oh, that’s because you hate fun, she could have said. Glinda’s is for people who know how to smile also crossed her mind, even as she remembered Taliesin’s knowing grin. Instead, she found herself saying, “If you stop by, tell Glinda I sent you. She keeps a special stash of lavender candies behind the counter for me at exam time.”


“Why lavender?”


“It’s soothing.” She held out one of the candies. “Calms the nerves.”


He took the candy from her, his fingers grazing her palm, and suddenly the air felt full of static, like their sweaters could spark and ignite. She held her breath as Taliesin unwrapped the pale purple cellophane and placed the candy on his tongue, sucking on it and swirling it around in his mouth. Maggie couldn’t stop staring at the way his lips pursed together as he sucked on the candy.


“Is it working?” she asked in a breathy whisper she barely recognized. She had no clue what was happening between them. His own gaze was trained on her mouth as she licked her lips. She couldn’t breathe.


He just hummed his assent, not taking his eyes off her mouth.


This was a hard lurch toward something she didn’t want to acknowledge. It was electric. It was inconvenient.


Maggie wished she could say she was the one who broke the gaze between them, but it was Taliesin. He tore his eyes from her lips like it pained him to do it and turned back around. For a moment, Maggie just stared at the back of his neck, at his shoulders, at the comical way his legs scrunched beneath his desk, breathing deeply. The way he’d been looking at her, the way he rolled that tongue over the candy, the ghost of his hand still between her shoulder blades, and the strange charge between them…She wanted him to turn back around, lean across her desk, and just kiss her to put her out of her misery. And where had that come from? So she picked up her bags and left without saying goodbye.


The next day, her cart was completely restocked. There were a dozen more Mothman stress balls, two full bags of lavender candy, and a third of Glinda’s newest flavor, chamomile. Taliesin had even bought a few dozen honey sticks and brought a handful of Glinda’s free stickers that she made of her shop logo, a black cat in an old-fashioned witch hat. Her students would love those. And there, lying on her desk, was a delicate sprig of lavender, wrapped in a pretty cream-colored ribbon. Maggie picked it up, running her fingers along the grosgrain. The flower’s calming smell lingered on the dried blooms. An echo, a memory.


She hung the lavender by its ribbon on her bookshelf, and every time she caught the sprig out of the corner of her eye, she furrowed her brow and told herself another lie. It’s just the small space. The office was too tight, too close. He was impossible to ignore. A couple of flirty texts, a sprig of lavender…you’re reaching, Maggie. But she wasn’t inventing the strange pull between them, or the desire she felt building every time she thought about kissing Arthur Taliesin.


It didn’t seem possible that she was consuming his thoughts the way Taliesin consumed hers. It was embarrassing how little she could concentrate when he was around. Her eyes were always drawn to his lips, his hands. She wanted to get close to him just to catch a hint of his cologne. The man barely looked at her with anything but dismay and dismissal at worst, curiosity at best. Another lie. She’d remind herself of the tender way he’d held her arm after the ghoul attack or the way he stared at her lips as if all he wanted, too, was a taste, and she would confuse herself again.


And if he was thinking about her the way she was thinking about him? It was irresponsible. She knew firsthand the damage that could come from getting involved with someone so entrenched in her daily life. She couldn’t put herself through that again. She wouldn’t.


She could think herself in circles about it, but on Thursday at Bean There, Done That, if he looked at her like that again, she would shut it down. She would have to.



—


For such a small town, Galloway somehow managed to be home to three coffee shops. Bean There, Done That was on the edge of downtown, three blocks north of Rodrigo’s. This extra distance away from her apartment meant she didn’t frequent it as much as one of the other two in town, but Bean There was warm and welcoming.


An unseasonable fire was roaring in a hearth to fight the pall’s damp chill, and there were wide booths and couches that made you want to sit and talk for hours, which was exactly what she and Taliesin needed. Maggie wouldn’t be leaving Bean There until she got some answers about the pall.


Taliesin sat tucked into a circular booth in the back corner, near the fire. He had covered the table with papers, file folders, and stacks of books. This late in the day, with the morning rush long over and the evening crowd already thinning, she hoped the employees didn’t mind if they spread out a bit, but she made a mental note to leave an extra-large tip.


Taliesin didn’t notice her come in, and she took a moment to watch him. He looked down at one of his papers with intense concentration, chewing on his lip absentmindedly. The fire reflected in his glasses, and his hair fell across his forehead. He picked up a book, scanning the text and tucking the paper he’d been reading between its pages, perhaps making some connection that he would want to reference later.


After a moment, he took off his glasses and rubbed his eyes. Even now, nearly a week after his bout of pall sickness, he still looked exhausted.


Maggie’s palms were sweating. They had spent weeks together, sitting within two feet of each other, but this felt different. Closer. Knees knocking beneath the table, elbows and shoulders brushing, shared breath over the top of the table as they looked through papers. Her cheeks burned at this wholly imagined scenario, but the past week had been confusing. Would she get the insufferable Taliesin who drove her to distraction? The charming man she’d caught glimpses of? Or the one who seemed to be drawn to her in the same fevered way she was drawn to him?


It had been a long time since she’d felt anything like the lust that had burned through her earlier in the week, but it was easy to explain away. It was just his closeness, their small space. It was the stranger’s kiss on Beltane, which seemed to have opened a door she’d kept locked for years. She didn’t want to kiss Arthur Taliesin at all, she reasoned. She was just yearning for her masked man. She almost believed it, too.


Taliesin glanced at his watch and then looked toward the door. His face brightened when he saw her, like he was very much looking forward to this brainstorming session. His smile was wide, and she saw crinkles at the corners of his eyes. She had seen this version of Taliesin once before, but it had been two-dimensional. Now he was here before her in the flesh, and she hoped he couldn’t see the way her eyes had gone wide from across the room.


He abandoned his papers and books on the table. “Good afternoon.” His voice was strangely formal. For just a moment, his smile fell, and he gave a small shake of his head.


“Hey,” she responded, a completely uninspired greeting. “Um, I’m going to get a coffee.” She had a feeling she would regret it. It had been a long time since she’d been able to handle coffee after three in the afternoon, but there wasn’t much of a chance she’d get through this without something to do with her hands.


“It’s on me.” He walked with her over to the counter. “And don’t think I’ve forgotten about your cream cheese pastry. I already asked Liv to set one aside.” Liv? “What do you like to drink?”


She should insist that she pay for her own drink, but she hesitated for only a moment before replying, “A lavender iced latte, please.”


He grinned at her like they shared some kind of secret. “To calm your nerves?”


And then she was thinking about the way he’d rolled that damn lavender candy around on his tongue, but she managed to say, “I’m fine. What is there to be nervous about?”


Before he could answer, the woman behind the counter said, “Ready for another coffee, Artie?”


Maggie looked over at Taliesin and then behind him, searching for the Artie she was speaking to. Arthur Taliesin looked less like an Artie than anyone she had ever met in her life.


After he ordered their drinks, the woman spoke over the hiss of the milk steamer. “You’re spoiling me today. It’s been too long since we last saw you.”


“Sorry, Liv.” There was a slight strain in his voice, as if he didn’t feel completely comfortable. “Things have been a little hectic.”


Maggie busied herself with looking at the pastries behind the glass—cherry tarts, blueberry lemon scones, slices of chocolate pie—as Liv continued to talk while she made their drinks. “Did you hear about the ghoul attack at Rodrigo’s?” Maggie looked up, and Taliesin glanced her way, eyebrows arching behind his glasses. Liv went on. “Two patrons managed to banish it before it caused too much damage, but…” She shivered theatrically. Taliesin looked like he was about to interrupt and announce that the patron herself was standing in Liv’s coffee shop, but Maggie shook her head.


Liv slid their drinks across the counter and then crouched behind the pastry cabinet as she went on. “It’s certainly been strange out there. The wardsmiths came by earlier this week and blamed it all on something out of the ordinary going on up at the Wilds. They shored up our storeroom wards for free, thank the gods above. Is the school doing anything about it?”


Taliesin’s smile tightened almost imperceptibly. “Trust me, they’re working on it.” His voice had an edge to it that Maggie had heard before but couldn’t quite read.


When Liv moved on, he visibly relaxed. “How are your dad and the boys?”


“Same old, same old.” He wasn’t looking at Liv as he said it, though. Instead, he was watching Maggie take her coffee, his gaze dipping down to her fingers as they brushed his. He seemed to be watching her expression for something, but she wasn’t sure what. She wondered if he found it when he gave her a small smile before turning back to Liv.


Maggie didn’t think Taliesin noticed, but Liv’s eyes darted between them as if she was trying to figure out just who Maggie was to him. Taliesin didn’t bother to introduce her, though, and Maggie wasn’t sure if she was annoyed by it or not.


“Pop’s been taking Simon out fishing on Saturday mornings,” he went on. Simon must be his nephew, then. “And Rory is Rory, you know.”


Liv chuckled as if she absolutely did know what Rory is Rory meant. Before they turned back to their tables, Taliesin reached into his pocket and dropped a twenty-dollar bill into the tip jar on the counter. “Ridiculous!” Liv shouted at him.


“Take it, Liv,” he insisted.


“I wasn’t going to give it back,” she said with a wink as Taliesin moved to return to their seats.


Maggie tried to make sense of everything she just heard as she slid into the booth that Taliesin had commandeered. She took a sip of her coffee and finally asked, as casually as she could, “So, how do you know Liv?”


He shrugged. “I’ve been doing my grading here. I’m always too tired to do it after the long drive back to Atlantia.”


That didn’t quite answer Maggie’s question. She wondered for a moment if she was being too nosy, but decided the disappointment Dahlia would feel if she didn’t get as much information from Taliesin as possible was not worth it. “But how does she know your dad?”


“Oh!” He seemed startled by her question, as if he thought the answer should be very obvious. “Liv went to high school with my brother, Rory.”


“Across the country?” Maggie asked, surprised. As far as she knew, Arthur had lived in Soladia up until last August, which was almost three thousand miles away from Bean There, Done That. “I thought your mom, Rowena…” she said and then stopped. She didn’t know Rowena Taliesin, and it was weird to refer to her by her first name. “I mean, Dr. Taliesin…” But that was weird, too, so she added a hasty, “Senior…gods below,” she muttered, completely floundering.


Despite her stumbling, Taliesin smiled. “It’s okay,” he said. “I grew up in Soladia with my mom, but my dad and half brother have always lived here.”


“Here?” Maggie was shocked by this news. “In Galloway?”


“Well, in Atlantia,” he clarified. It was like the missing puzzle piece finally clicking into place. That was why he was living in Atlantia instead of Galloway. This must be why he’d left prestigious Dartwood for Hawthorn.


“I had no idea.”


Taliesin wrapped his hands around his coffee, his broad shoulders bunched into his ears as he shrugged. “You didn’t ask. It’s not something most people know about me.”


“Why not?”


He looked at Maggie before he answered, his gaze lingering on her lips for just a second. But then he sighed and said, “Most people just want to know about Rowena Taliesin, the legendary alchemist. If they want to know about me, it’s about my research or one of the projects I consulted on.” Quickly he added, “Which I’m not complaining about! It’s nice when people are curious about my work. But there is rarely much curiosity left for the rest of me.”


Maggie’s cheeks warmed. She hadn’t expected such a candid answer. Had she done that? Made him feel like he didn’t matter? Before the pall, she hadn’t had many conversations with Taliesin beyond welcoming him to the university in the fall. “I’m sorry if I ever made you feel that way,” she said, and she hoped he could hear the sincerity in her voice.


His expression softened. “Never you, Maggie. You just yell at me.”


“Oh, well…” She wasn’t sure if that was better. “I promise I don’t usually yell at colleagues.”


He smirked. “Just me, then?” His voice was low and Maggie’s cheeks turned redder, but she couldn’t bring herself to deny it.
